examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/558cbc7aba862d44e34a7b109ea84c1f7a6f3f1f4b505e5f476e62a29fdd654b.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

- From the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/ca2243ed8015927b9db5428d676ee59907264fc223721246a81b2e73aca3b351.png) we deduce that $\textrm{Re}(\lambda)={\color{blue}3}$ and $\textrm{Im}(\lambda) = {\color{red}-1}.$ So, our eigenvalue is

$$
\lambda = {\color{blue}3}+({\color{red}-1})\text{i} = 3-\text{i}.
$$

- From the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/7a5bb57b71eb218271f2bb0ab718304d6b834738f1004eac7c501a7fd4ffa2b3.png) we deduce that our corresponding eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/0ea51255e7594236cdd5d8dee0997f64b49f77cbb77e8cfd97937830a862283b.png)

Finally, the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda,$ and the second eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Therefore, our eigenvalues and eigenvectors are
